Why It Matters

Why Steel Thickness Is the Most Important Spec

A determined burglar with a reciprocating saw can cut through 14-gauge steel in under two minutes. That same saw against .22-inch (4-gauge) steel? It's a significantly longer, louder, and more difficult job — enough to deter most attacks entirely.

Steel thickness determines:

How long the safe resists cutting tools
How much force is needed to pry the door
How much the safe weighs (heavier = harder to remove)
How long the safe protects contents in a fire (more steel = more thermal mass)
.075" Typical big-box safe body — 14 gauge, cut in under 2 minutes
.224" Sturdy Heavy Duty body — 4 gauge, nearly 3× thicker, significantly harder to defeat
3/8" Sturdy door plate — the thickest standard door plate in the residential safe market

Why Fire Insulation Material Matters

Why Fire Insulation Material Matters More Than Fire Rating

There is no regulated standard for "fire ratings" in the gun safe industry. A manufacturer can claim "2 hours at 1,800°F" with no independent testing required. The only thing you can verify is the insulation material:

Frequently Asked Questions

Common Questions

A big-box safe is better than no safe for preventing casual access. But for protection against determined theft, tools, or house fires, the thin steel and drywall insulation in most big-box safes is significantly less effective than what's available at a similar or slightly higher price point.

The starting price difference (roughly $1,000–$2,000) reflects 3× thicker steel, ceramic wool insulation, continuous hot welds, and a lifetime warranty with the deductible guarantee. The average gun collection is worth $5,000–$25,000 — the safe that protects it is not the place to cut costs.

Steel gauge is a standard measurement where lower numbers mean thicker steel. 4 gauge (.22") is nearly twice as thick as 12 gauge (.109"). The difference determines how long your safe resists pry bars, power tools, and cutting wheels. Most big-box safes use 12 to 14 gauge steel. Our Heavy Duty line starts at 4 gauge.

With enough time and the right tools, yes. The goal is to make the attack take long enough that it is not worth attempting — or to require tools that most burglars don't carry. Our Heavy Duty safes resist the attack methods used in real-world residential burglaries. Most big-box safes can be opened with a pry bar in under five minutes.

The math is straightforward. A $600 big-box safe that gets pried open in a burglary costs you everything inside plus replacement. A Sturdy Safe that is never defeated costs what you paid — one time. When your contents include firearms, documents, and irreplaceable items, the price difference is not close.
